title: IAF chief tells US general: no official F-35 offer, India still waiting
excerpt: At the close of Exercise Tarang Shakti-2026 in Jodhpur, Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh said Washington has never formally offered the F-35 — while Russia's Su-57 pitch also awaits a decision.
body:
• Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh said the United States has made no official offer to sell F-35 stealth fighters to India, telling the US Pacific Air Forces commander: "Your people don't even let us go near the aircraft, and you are talking about selling it to us."
  • The remarks came at the concluding press conference of Exercise Tarang Shakti-2026 in Jodhpur, where six US Air Force F-35As took part — the jet's first appearance in a military exercise on Indian soil.
  • Singh said Russia has offered its Su-57 fighter, but no decision has been made on whether the IAF will even evaluate it.
  • The comments land a week after Singh warned that delays to India's indigenous AMCA programme could force the air force to look at foreign fifth-generation options.

The lead

The head of the Indian Air Force has said, in plain terms, that Washington has never formally offered India the F-35 — and he said it sitting next to the American general who brought the jets to India. "Your people don't even let us go near the aircraft, and you are talking about selling it to us," Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh quipped at the closing press conference of Exercise Tarang Shakti-2026 in Jodhpur on Saturday, with US Pacific Air Forces commander Gen. Kevin Schneider seated alongside him.

The exchange underscored the gap between the rhetoric around a possible F-35 sale and anything on paper. In February 2025, US President Donald Trump told a joint press conference with Prime Minister Narendra Modi that his administration was "paving the way" to provide India with F-35 stealth fighters. More than a year and a half later, no proposal has arrived through the US Foreign Military Sales programme, and Singh has now confirmed publicly that no official offer exists.

"Your people don't even let us go near the aircraft, and you are talking about selling it to us."

— Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh, IAF Chief, at the Tarang Shakti-2026 concluding press conference

The context

The venue gave Singh's remarks their edge. Six US Air Force F-35As, supported by more than 200 personnel, had just finished their stint at Tarang Shakti-2026 — the first time the F-35 has participated in a military exercise on Indian soil. Indian officials got a close look at how the fifth-generation jet operates alongside IAF fighters, but American security protocols kept them at arm's length from the aircraft itself. The F-35 had previously been showcased at Aero India in Bengaluru in February 2025.

IAF officials say the exercise let Indian pilots study the stealth signatures of fifth-generation combat jets — operational intelligence that stands apart from any procurement question.

The F-35 pitch has always sat uneasily with India's defence calculus. New Delhi operates Russian S-400 air defence regiments, bought in a $5.5 billion deal in 2018, and Washington's protocols — shaped by CAATSA sanctions law and ITAR arms-transfer rules — treat operating the F-35 near Russian radars as a non-starter. Turkey was expelled from the F-35 programme after buying the S-400, a precedent Indian planners know well. There is also the Make in India factor: an F-35 deal would almost certainly be a direct sale with tight US end-user monitoring, at odds with India's push for domestic production.

The Su-57 question

Singh also addressed the other half of the fifth-generation conversation. Russia has offered India its Su-57 fighter, he said, but the government and the IAF have not decided whether to evaluate it. Any assessment, he added, would depend on how well the aircraft meets the IAF's requirements.

"No decision has been made on whether to evaluate the Su-57. Any assessment would depend on how well the aircraft meets the IAF's requirements."

— Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh, IAF Chief

The caution fits a pattern. At his annual press conference on October 3, ahead of Air Force Day, Singh warned that India's indigenous Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) programme is running behind schedule, with the first prototype now expected to fly around 2028. He said the air force may have to consider alternative fifth-generation platforms if the AMCA slips further. That admission matters: the IAF is down to 29 fighter squadrons against an authorised strength of 42, and deliveries of the indigenous Tejas Mk-1A are running late, held up by supply-chain constraints on its GE engines.

Still, the defence establishment keeps repeating its official line. Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh has said India is not in formal consultations on either the F-35 or the Su-57 and remains committed to the AMCA as the country's primary fifth-generation solution.

The diaspora angle

For the Indian diaspora in the United States, the story is a window into how New Delhi is navigating its defence ties with Washington — enthusiastic about joint exercises and interoperability, but unwilling to bend procurement to American terms. The outcome of the fighter question will shape US-India defence cooperation for decades.

What's next

With Tarang Shakti-2026 concluded, the ball is in no one's court — which is Singh's point. There is no FMS offer to respond to, no Su-57 evaluation team constituted, and no revised AMCA timeline announced. The IAF's squadron shortfall is getting worse by the year, so the question of a foreign fifth-generation stopgap will keep returning. What is settled is only what Singh said in Jodhpur: talk of selling the F-35 to India is, for now, just talk.
